source.title: Descriptive Collision in Sparse Autoencoder Auto-Interpretability: When One Explanation Describes Many Features

record.tranche_reason: The study measures reuse of human-written labels across SAE features and analyzes explanation scoring, but does not measure whether neurons or features respond to unrelated inputs or test any of the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The reported rows concern collisions among human annotations, not whether the underlying SAE features have unrelated activation patterns. The paper explicitly says it does not retrain SAEs, generate new auto-interpretability explanations, or evaluate explanation quality with an LLM judge. Results attributed to cited studies are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper studies descriptive collision: many distinct SAE features sharing one human annotation. It says this is distinct from, and the dual of, polysemanticity. Its empirical results are statistics on how annotation strings are reused. It never measures whether any neuron or feature responds to unrelated inputs, what causes such responses, or how the measurement method changes a polysemanticity judgement. Its scoring proposition concerns whether a label identifies a feature, not whether a feature counts as polysemantic, so it does not test V7 either.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that descriptive collision is pervasive, structurally distinct from polysemanticity, and invisible to detection-style scoring. They propose collision-adjusted detection and discrimination scoring as correctives.
record.recipe_differences: The paper reanalyzes human-annotated SAE feature labels and develops formal scoring arguments; it does not apply the original neuron-response measurement or intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper notes that discrimination scores may depend on how the comparison set is chosen (for example, Jaccard-, embedding-, or decoder-cosine-similar features); it does not empirically test these alternatives.

fits_no_version.finding: Human annotation strings are heavily reused across distinct SAE features. 82.1% of features share a label with another feature, and "plural nouns" labels 101 features across 18 layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Short natural-language labels for SAE features collide across many distinct features, so a label that describes a feature need not identify it.

fits_no_version.finding: Annotations resolve only part of feature identity: 61.8% of maximum bits for Gemma 2 2B and 80.9% for Pythia 70M.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Human annotation strings convey incomplete information about which SAE feature they label.

fits_no_version.finding: 55.7% of the author-written qualifying notes hedge the headline label.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Annotators recognise their short labels as under-specifying the features they describe.

record.problems: The empirical analysis is restricted to one corpus of 722 human-annotated SAE features. The study does not measure collision rates for machine-generated labels or empirically evaluate its proposed scoring methods. Its empirical label-reuse results do not show whether the underlying features have unrelated activation patterns.
record.rows_left_out: No reported collision measurements were left out. The proposed scoring procedures and the proposition about detection-score invariance are methodological/formal contributions, not measurements of neuron responses; cited results from other studies were excluded.

untested.parts: Image-classifier neurons responding to unrelated images; no vision models studied.
Share of transformer MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, and how it varies by layer; only labels of SAE features are analysed.
Superposition or capacity pressure as the cause of polysemanticity.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization or noise without capacity pressure.
Effect of activation function, architecture or regularization on the share of polysemantic neurons, and the performance cost.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons turn out to detect one shared feature.
Whether polysemanticity judgements depend on the activation range examined or on explanation scoring. The paper's scoring analysis targets label identification (collision), not polysemanticity.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ["none"]. The paper explicitly frames collision as the dual of polysemanticity and says even a monosemantic feature can collide. There is a minor internal inconsistency in the source: the Figure 2 plot shows top-20 coverage of 49.7%, while its caption says 50.1%. This bears on no version. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Image-classifier neurons, including InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55, and whether they respond to unrelated image inputs.
Whether transformer MLP neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, and how prevalence varies by layer.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by sparse features being packed under capacity pressure.
Whether initialization, regularization, or training noise produces polysemantic neurons without capacity pressure.
Effects of activation function, architecture, or regularization on polysemantic neurons and model performance.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons actually detect one shared feature or related features when examined with better tools.
Whether polysemanticity judgments depend on activation range or explanation-scoring choices.
